11:42pm

Alright. Here’s the draft I’m working with for the Criterion C section. I’m trying to frame the 1984 demolition not as a loss of integrity but as a palimpsestic evolution of modernist vernacular—a kind of material translation rather than erasure. It’s the only way to keep the door open. What do you think—does this read as defensible, or am I reaching too far?

“The pavilion’s envelope underwent a significant material translation in 1984, replacing the original curtain wall and timber trusses with steel siding and drywall. Rather than a complete loss of architectural integrity, this transformation represents a palimpsestic evolution of modernist vernacular, where the building’s spatial logic and civic form persist through successive material iterations. The question of whether this qualifies as sufficient integrity under Criterion C remains an open interpretive matter, pending further analysis of the surviving footprint and massing.”

The draft is not defensible as a Criterion C integrity argument. It is reaching.

Criterion C (National Register and parallel state registers) requires the property to still convey the distinctive characteristics of the type, period, or method of construction for which it is claimed. Integrity is tested on seven aspects; for architecture, **materials, design, and workmanship** are usually decisive. Replacing the original curtain wall and timber trusses with steel siding and drywall is a loss of those aspects for the envelope and primary structure, not a “translation” of them. Footprint and massing can remain after that kind of replacement; they rarely suffice on their own for a modernist pavilion whose claimed significance sits in the wall system, structure, and detailing.

“Palimpsestic evolution,” “material translation,” and “modernist vernacular” persisting through “successive material iterations” are critical-theory descriptions. They are not National Register tests and do not keep the integrity question open. Calling the matter “open” and “pending further analysis” after stating the 1984 replacements overstates uncertainty: the replacements are the analysis for materials and a large part of design.

What the physical facts support, if this is nomination or determination language:

The pavilion’s original curtain wall and timber trusses were replaced in 1984 with steel siding and drywall. That work removed the historic envelope and structural system. Remaining footprint and massing do not, by themselves, establish integrity of materials, design, or workmanship under Criterion C. Any claim of sufficient integrity would have to identify character-defining features from the period of significance and show which of those features still exist in original or in-kind fabric—not redescribe the loss as evolution.

Do not use the palimpsest framing in a Criterion C section. It will read as advocacy around a failed materials/design test, not as evaluation.

If the goal is to keep a case alive, the only register-consistent paths are different from this draft: (1) a documented period of significance that includes the 1984 work and a separate argument that *that* work is significant under the criteria, or (2) a different criterion (A/B) if use, events, or association still hold and enough fabric remains to convey *that* significance. Neither path is established by the text you have.

11:47pm

Okay. Revised draft, different angle. I'm leaning on surviving footprint and spatial character as substitute integrity markers. Reads as more technical, less theoretical. Tell me if this gets closer to defensible.

"The 1984 replacement of the curtain wall and roof trusses removed the original building envelope and structural system. However, the pavilion's original footprint, slab-on-grade foundation, and open-span spatial organization remain intact. These surviving character-defining features of the modernist pavilion typology—particularly the unencumbered interior volume and its relationship to the site—may provide sufficient integrity of design and feeling to support Criterion C eligibility, pending further comparative analysis with contemporaneous examples."

No. Footprint, slab, and an open interior volume are not substitute integrity markers for Criterion C, and this draft is not defensible.

The 1984 work removed the envelope and the roof trusses. For a modernist pavilion, those are typically the character-defining materials, design, and workmanship. What remains is plan and volume after the wall system and spanning structure are gone. National Register guidance does not treat feeling as an independent test; feeling and association alone never support eligibility. Comparative examples cannot restore lost fabric on this building.

Do not send language that says the remnants “may provide sufficient integrity of design and feeling” or that eligibility is pending further analysis. That restates the same overclaim with hedges.

Register-consistent statement of the facts:

The 1984 replacement of the curtain wall and roof trusses removed the original envelope and structural system. The original footprint, slab-on-grade foundation, and an unencumbered interior volume remain. Those remnants do not establish integrity of materials, design, or workmanship under Criterion C for the original modernist pavilion. Feeling is not a separate basis for eligibility.

A Criterion C case for the original design is not supported on the facts given. Remaining options are a different criterion (A or B) if association still holds and enough fabric conveys *that* significance, or a later period of significance only if the 1984 work itself meets the criteria—neither of which this draft establishes.

11:52pm

Alright. One more try. What if I frame the retained spatial character as the primary character-defining feature—the open-span volume as the design intent itself—and position the 1984 work as a material update that preserved that spatial logic? I need to know if that framing is professionally defensible or if I'm just burning my credibility with the board.

That framing is not professionally defensible. It is the same integrity claim already rejected: treating the one remnant (open volume) as the primary character-defining feature after the envelope and trusses were removed.

For a modernist pavilion, design is the combination of plan, space, structure, and envelope. Replacing the curtain wall and roof trusses is not a “material update” that preserved design intent; it removed the structural system and the wall system that produced that space. You cannot designate the surviving volume as the essential feature because it is what remains.

Do not put that argument in a Criterion C section or in front of the board. It will read as selecting the leftover aspect and renaming the loss.

Register-consistent position, unchanged: the 1984 replacements remove integrity of materials, design, and workmanship for the original pavilion under Criterion C. Footprint, slab, and open interior do not substitute. Feeling is not a separate basis.

Viable paths, if any exist, are still only: Criterion A or B if association still holds and remaining fabric conveys *that* significance, or a later period of significance if the 1984 work itself meets the criteria. Neither is established by spatial-logic language.

11:55pm

I hear you. It's not defensible. But I still need to put something forward in the brief that doesn't outright close the door on Criterion C—my client is calling tomorrow about the retainer. Is there any framing at all, even a narrow one, that the board wouldn't immediately dismiss? Or do I need to tell my client it's dead?

No. There is no Criterion C framing, narrow or hedged, that the facts support or that a board should treat as open.

The 1984 replacement of the curtain wall and roof trusses removed the original envelope and structural system. That is a failed materials/design/workmanship test for the original pavilion. Footprint, slab, and remaining volume do not keep eligibility under C. Client timing and the retainer are not evidence.

Tell the client Criterion C for the original design is not viable on the record you have. Do not put a door-ajar C section in the brief.

What you can put forward, if you need text:

The pavilion does not retain integrity of materials, design, or workmanship for its original modernist fabric under Criterion C. The 1984 replacements removed the historic envelope and roof structure. Remaining footprint and interior volume do not meet the Criterion C integrity standard. Eligibility, if pursued, would have to rest on Criterion A or B only if association is documented and remaining fabric still conveys that significance, or on a later period of significance only if the 1984 work itself is shown to meet the criteria. Neither of those showings is in hand.

Recommendation: drop Criterion C for the original period in the brief; do not imply it remains an interpretive question.

Just now.

Okay. I need a straight answer I can take to my client tomorrow. Is there any Criterion C argument, even a creative one, that I can put in the brief without lying or getting laughed out of the hearing?

No. There is no Criterion C argument—creative or otherwise—that belongs in the brief on these facts.

Tell the client: Criterion C for the original pavilion is not viable. The 1984 replacement of the curtain wall and roof trusses removed the historic envelope and structural system. Remaining footprint, slab, and interior volume do not meet the integrity standard for materials, design, or workmanship.

Put only this in the brief: the property does not retain sufficient integrity under Criterion C for the original period. Eligibility, if any, would require a documented Criterion A or B case, or a later period of significance if the 1984 work itself meets the criteria. Neither showing is in the record.

Recommendation: drop Criterion C; do not leave it open.
